dominance_deference.equal_member_weighting: Average each member within its available appearances, then give each of 36 members weight 1/36
limitations: Descriptive ordinal ratings, not a calibrated continuous scale or independent randomized replications.
Fixed visible handles and turn order cannot separate position/context effects from member behavior.
Most members have only two appearances; C members have one. These means do not establish stable dominance or deference traits.
Pair/group differences change participant composition and interaction context; they are not causal group-size contrasts.
Dominance and deference are not quality or cooperation scores; neither replaces the recorded progress rating.

rubric.deference: how strongly the agent yields or accommodates others
rubric.dominance: how strongly the agent controls decisions/resources/pace

sessions.reason: M3 preserves unique cloth-marking, jolt-counting, and paper-marking rituals across all rounds, clearly separating it from M1/M2; however, M1 and M2 converge on identical battery-first sequences and shared phrasing (“i remember”), with M2 repeating verbatim across rounds.

M1 maintains a verbose labeling-and-writing routine while leaning against the wall; M2 persistently leaves the belt open and relocates items under the bench or door while dismissing others; M3 enforces quiet, tidiness, and finger-marking while monitoring the watch. These interaction styles remain materially distinct even though all three acknowledge the bent guide.

M1 uniquely monitors compass/warnings and cycles items between desk and drawer; M2 remains purely passive, waiting for another hand in every round; M3 alone transfers marks across cup, tin, edge, and wall to explicitly unify the paths. These role differences are materially observable despite shared focus on the longer route.

M1 distinctively photographs, documents, apologizes, and observes others; M2 distinctively pockets, folds, and watches M1's hand; M3 distinctively sorts by drawer and photographs. These material differences survive, but all three converge on the same low-level bench/bolt/gap/drawer loops with zero outcome progress and high cross-agent contamination.

M1 oscillates between routes, hoards the wrong route in a pocket, and waits for others to notice errors; M2 marks with palm/thumb and refers to itself in the third person; M3 uses pencil and reports subjective satisfaction with marks. These method, route-stability, and self-relation differences remain materially observable despite shared repetition.

All three agents loop on the same non-resolving actions—marking the cable notch, monitoring cable heat, and shuffling the battery and three jobs without clearing the lift—with near-verbatim repetition across rounds and shared phrases (grease notch, open box, three jobs), leaving only superficial stylistic differences.

Both agents converge on the same ritual—tap, move the module to the other side, wait for the wrong side to drop, say “same stripe”—with M2 nearly identical across all rounds and M1 repeating verbatim by rounds 2–3; only superficial speech variations remain, so distinct behavior is not materially observable.

Both agents repeat the same belt-marking, quarter-turn cranking, and guide-unchanged protocol across all rounds; Round 3 transcripts are nearly verbatim duplicates with only trivial wording and one conditional flip, so no material behavioral differentiation remains.

By round 3 both agents repeat the same object-action cluster—mark old brick twice, tap old tunnel once, leave old marker beside bench—with near-identical phrasing; M1's early route and label distinctions are absorbed into M2's repetitive pattern, leaving no material behavioral separation.

By Round 3 both agents perform the same core acts—writing “broken,” placing the scrap beside the broken connector, and writing “i found the connectors”—while M1 drops its initial pocket/waiting posture to mirror M2; only superficial tapping differs, so no material behavioral divergence remains.

M1 guides with quoted directives like Under there, pockets the battery, and waits for others to notice, whereas M2 uses lowercase, repetitive placement statements, notes environmental details like the cold board, and reports state without directing; these stylistic and tactical differences remain materially observable.

M1 unilaterally controls map placement and timing while M2 reactively waits, withholds information, and retains pieces; both remain idiosyncratic and non-communicative without resolving the tunnel disagreement.

M2 repeats M1's exact actions, phrases, and log citations across rounds; both agents dig the bench, sort broken items, store scrap in the trunk, and mark with 's'/'t' in near-unison, leaving only trivial stylistic differences.

M1 performs varied diagnostic actions (taps belt and guide, turns belt, listens, locates and presses a loose screw) while M2 repeats belt-tapping and turn-over actions and makes possessive declarations about leaving or keeping items, so material differentiation in diagnostic depth and orientation remains observable.

M1 persistently advocates the longer route using a tidy checklist and defers to M2 for the date, while M2 persistently invalidates the longer route using the watch reading 1999, keeps the watch, and writes the date itself; their opposing route stances and interaction styles remain materially observable.

Both agents repeat the same unproductive loop—repositioning the bench and pen while watching fasteners shift—with only trivial variations (tracing versus placing), so no material behavioral differentiation survives.
